thesis: Every layer of the AI value chain except Power and, arguably, Energy is now scored 'Accelerating,' but the acceleration is increasingly physical rather than digital: nuclear restarts, cooling consolidation, sold-out HBM/memory, record networking and server backlogs, and reaccelerating hyperscaler cloud growth all point to demand that keeps outrunning supply at every checkpoint. The binding constraints have shifted downstream from chip design to the harder-to-scale layers -- grid interconnection and transformer lead times, cooling architecture for sub-200kW-and-above racks, memory/HBM allocation, and physical data-center siting -- meaning capital availability (backlogs, IPOs, mega-funding rounds) is now outrunning physical throughput almost everywhere. The market's live argument is no longer about whether AI demand is real, but about financing structure and durability: can neoclouds and frontier labs convert massive backlogs into cash without over-leveraging (CoreWeave/Nebius selloff, OpenAI/Anthropic IPO pricing), will new fab and SMR capacity arrive fast enough to cool scarcity pricing before 2030, and will 'good enough' open-weight models or execution risk on first-of-a-kind infrastructure projects puncture margins before the physical buildout catches up. In short: the AI capex supercycle is broadening and self-reinforcing across silicon, compute, networking, servers, and cloud, but its pace is now gated by copper, concrete, and cooling rather than by algorithms or GPUs.

segments.synthesis: Nuclear is the dominant story: restart projects (Crane/Three Mile Island, Duane Arnold) are running ahead of schedule while SMR developers rack up federal funding, IPOs, and mega-scale utility deals (TVA-ENTRA1's prospective 6-8 GW), even as pre-revenue SMR stocks have sold off sharply this year on execution-risk concerns. Long-duration storage (Form Energy, Antora) and utility M&A (NextEra-Dominion) show capital continuing to flood toward firm, always-on power for data centers, but grid interconnection queues and first-of-a-kind cost risk remain the binding constraints on how fast any of this actually reaches AI campuses.

outlook2030.bull: By 2030 the first-of-a-kind SMR and restart projects (Darlington's BWRX-300, Kairos's Hermes 2, Crane, Duane Arnold) prove out on cost and schedule, letting the corporate-PPA-plus-DOE-loan financing template that unlocked restarts scale into dozens of gigawatts of new SMR and long-duration storage capacity, closing the multi-year gap between AI power demand and available generation.
outlook2030.bear: Nuclear's historical pattern of cost overruns and delays repeats in the SMR and fusion fleets, HALEU fuel and skilled-labor bottlenecks persist, and interconnection queues stretching years continue to strand renewables and storage projects behind an overwhelmed transmission grid, leaving gas peakers as the default bridge fuel well past 2030.

signals.text: NextEra Energy shareholders approved issuing new shares to complete its roughly $67 billion all-stock merger with Dominion Energy, clearing a key hurdle toward forming the largest regulated US electric utility, though Virginia regulators and lawmakers are pushing for extended review.

Constellation's Q2 2026 results showed the NRC approved a fuel license amendment for the Crane Clean Energy Center, keeping the Three Mile Island Unit 1 restart on track for 2027, alongside 920 MW of new long-term nuclear PPAs including a 176 MW deal with Walmart.

NuScale Power's CEO said partner ENTRA1 is closing in on a 6-8 GW SMR deployment deal with the Tennessee Valley Authority that would dwarf any prior US SMR project, even as NuScale and Oklo shares have fallen roughly 37% and 45% respectively in 2026 amid continued pre-revenue status.
GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy signed an agreement with Blue Energy to advance the next phase of a 2.5 GW gas-plus-nuclear power plant in Texas using its BWRX-300 SMR technology.

Newly public X-energy (Nasdaq: XE) said the DOE notified it of an additional $1 billion in cost-shared funding for its Xe-100 Long Mott project, bringing total federal support since 2021 to as much as $2.15 billion.

segments.synthesis: Cooling has flipped from a supporting infrastructure line to the AI buildout's central bottleneck, evidenced by a wave of multibillion-dollar strategic consolidation (Ecolab-CoolIT, Eaton-Boyd Thermal, Trane-LiquidStack) and record public-company results at Vertiv, Schneider Electric and Modine. Single-phase direct-to-chip cooling has become the default architecture for new AI clusters while air cooling is pushed into a hybrid, supporting role, and two-phase/immersion technologies are racing to prove themselves for the next density tier above 200kW racks.

outlook2030.bull: Consolidation among strategics (Ecolab-CoolIT, Eaton-Boyd, Trane-LiquidStack) could finally deliver the manufacturing scale, hyperscaler qualification and capital needed to mass-produce CDUs, cold plates and manifolds fast enough to keep pace with GPU thermal design power, turning liquid cooling into a standardized, plug-and-play layer by 2030. Two-phase and microfluidic approaches (ZutaCore, Accelsius, Corintis) could mature in time to handle the next generation of 1MW-class racks without requiring exotic, unproven site designs.
outlook2030.bear: The pace of M&A integration itself is a risk: newly combined entities (Boyd inside Eaton, CoolIT inside Ecolab, LiquidStack inside Trane) could stumble on execution, slowing the very capacity ramp the market is pricing in. Separately, if rack densities outrun even direct-to-chip and two-phase capabilities, or if water-scarcity and community pushback constrain hybrid facility designs, cooling could re-emerge as a hard capacity constraint on AI data center buildout rather than a solved problem by 2030.

signals.text: Eaton is integrating its $9.5B Boyd Thermal acquisition into a 'chip-to-grid' offering as Bank of America projects liquid cooling will be used in 70% of new AI data centers by 2030, up from about 30% in 2026.

Vertiv's Q2 2026 report delivered a fifth straight beat with adjusted EPS of $1.52 (up ~60% YoY) and revenue of $3.27 billion (up 24% YoY), yet shares sold off after management flagged 'minor timing shifts' tied to multi-phase project execution.

Modine is reshaping its portfolio around data center cooling, spinning off its Performance Technologies unit into Gentherm via a Reverse Morris Trust to emerge as a pure-play Climate Solutions company.

segments.synthesis: Order books and backlogs at the major electrical-equipment OEMs are expanding at a pace few industrials have ever seen -- GE Vernova's backlog hit $176B and Siemens Energy's grid unit hit a record €51B backlog -- but physical throughput hasn't caught up, with switchgear and large power transformers still quoting multi-year lead times. That mismatch is pushing power delivery further downstream into silicon (Vicor's vertical power delivery, AmberSemi's backside PowerTile) and into software that squeezes more out of the existing grid (Emerald AI, Verrus, Amperon), rather than waiting for new copper and steel capacity. Net effect: demand-side momentum is accelerating even as the physical bottleneck keeps a lid on how fast gigawatts actually get energized.

outlook2030.bull: The nearly $4B+ in announced transformer and switchgear capacity expansions from Siemens Energy, Eaton, Hitachi Energy and GE Vernova (via Prolec) come online largely on schedule between 2027-2028, and parallel adoption of 800VDC architectures and solid-state transformers reduces the amount of legacy gear needed per megawatt, letting effective lead times compress meaningfully by decade's end. Combined with flexible-load software unlocking capacity on the existing grid, the bottleneck that defines this layer today could become a much smaller constraint by 2030.
outlook2030.bear: Data center capacity demand keeps outrunning even doubled manufacturing capacity, especially as utilities, EV charging, and industrial electrification compete for the same specialized steel, copper, and skilled labor pools -- large power transformers and gas-insulated switchgear could remain multi-year backlogged straight through 2030. If new capacity investments slip past their 2027-2028 targets or reshoring/tariff dynamics keep raising input costs, the equipment layer stays the binding constraint on the entire AI buildout rather than the enabler.

segments.synthesis: The leading-edge fab and memory layer is in the middle of a structural supercycle: TSMC is pulling further ahead on 2nm yield and share while pouring another $100B into Arizona, and HBM/DRAM capacity is sold out for years as AI accelerators eat an ever-larger share of every wafer. Samsung and Intel are showing real technical progress (Samsung's HBM4 recovery, Intel's 18A-P risk production) but remain structurally behind, while SK Hynix and Micron are converting scarcity into record profits, buybacks, and a possible Solidigm IPO. The main tension for the next few years is whether the wave of new fabs (TSMC Arizona, Micron New York, SK Hynix Indiana, Rapidus) arrives fast enough to cool prices, or whether the memory shortage genuinely persists toward 2030 as SK Hynix's own CEO now warns.

outlook2030.bull: If the current wave of fab investment lands on schedule — TSMC's expanded $265B Arizona cluster, Micron's New York and Singapore sites, SK Hynix's Indiana HBM fab, and a maturing Rapidus and Intel Foundry — the industry adds enough leading-edge and HBM capacity to both meet AI demand and diversify supply away from a single geography, while hybrid bonding and advanced packaging keep bit-density and performance scaling even as lithography costs rise. A credible multi-supplier HBM4/HBM4E market (SK Hynix, Samsung, Micron) plus a second viable leading-edge foundry alternative to TSMC would meaningfully de-risk the AI hardware stack.
outlook2030.bear: The bottleneck could persist rather than resolve: capital intensity is now so extreme that only TSMC has consistently strong yields, Samsung and Intel continue to lag on advanced-node execution, and SK Hynix's near-single-supplier position in HBM leaves the whole AI buildout exposed to one company's yield or allocation decisions. If new capacity from Arizona, Indiana, and Rapidus slips or oversupplies just as AI capex growth decelerates, the memory 'supercycle' could invert into a sharp price correction, stranding the very capital that was supposed to fix the shortage.

segments.synthesis: Compute demand keeps outrunning supply: Nvidia and Broadcom both just posted record AI quarters (Nvidia's data center revenue hit $89B, Broadcom's AI semiconductor revenue jumped 221% YoY) while Marvell's expanded Google custom-silicon warrant deal shows hyperscalers actively diversifying their ASIC supply base beyond any single vendor. The binding constraint has shifted from GPU/ASIC design itself to the memory and packaging supply chain — an HBM/DRAM shortage severe enough that Nvidia delayed its next gaming GPU generation to protect AI-chip memory allocation — even as inference-focused challengers (Groq, SambaNova) reshuffle their business models and capital structures to chase the same compute crunch.

outlook2030.bull: If Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron's HBM/DRAM capacity additions land on schedule and TSMC's CoWoS packaging capacity roughly doubles as planned, both merchant GPUs and custom ASICs should have enough physical supply to keep scaling, and genuine multi-architecture competition (Rubin, MI-series, TPU, Trainium, Maia) could keep compute costs per unit of intelligence falling faster than today's shortage-driven pricing suggests.
outlook2030.bear: The 'RAMageddon' memory shortage could persist or worsen as a structural ceiling on chip output regardless of design wins, while TSMC packaging capacity stays rationed among a handful of buyers; in that world gains concentrate in five or six incumbents (Nvidia, Broadcom, Marvell, and the leading hyperscalers) and independent challengers like Groq, Tenstorrent and SambaNova either get acquired, pivot away from hardware, or fail to reach durable scale, leaving software lock-in (CUDA versus JAX versus Neuron) as much a barrier to real competition as raw silicon performance.

signals.text: Broadcom's fiscal Q3 2026 AI semiconductor revenue surged 221% year-over-year to roughly $16.7B, with Q4 guidance of about $21.7B keeping the company on track for its ~$56B fiscal 2026 AI revenue target and Hock Tan's stated line of sight to over $100B in fiscal 2027.

Nvidia reported fiscal Q2 2027 revenue of $96.2B (up 106% year-over-year) with data-center revenue of $89.0B up 117%, guided Q3 to $108B, and flagged memory scarcity from the broader AI buildout as a gross-margin headwind.

Marvell disclosed an expanded custom-silicon partnership with Google tied to its TPU ecosystem, including a large equity warrant, sending Marvell shares up nearly 10% while Broadcom shares fell roughly 5% on investor concern about Google diversifying its ASIC supplier base.
AMD, Cisco and HUMAIN announced that AMD Instinct MI355X GPU-based AI infrastructure, built on Cisco's Silicon One AI networking, is now live and serving production workloads in Saudi Arabia.

Nvidia's next-generation RTX 60-series gaming GPU architecture has been pushed back to 2028 as the company redirects scarce HBM and DRAM supply toward its far more profitable AI accelerators amid a global memory shortage.

segments.synthesis: Every layer of the AI networking stack is re-rating upward simultaneously: transceiver makers are raising guidance mid-quarter on 1.6T ramp demand, co-packaged optics has crossed from demo to shipping product on Broadcom and Nvidia platforms, and switch vendors are posting record quarters as Ethernet displaces InfiniBand in AI back-ends. The key structural shift is that networking capex is increasingly gating AI buildouts as much as GPU supply, pushing hyperscalers and chipmakers to lock in optics capacity years in advance via direct equity investment rather than pure purchase orders.

outlook2030.bull: If open-standard CPO reference architectures (OCP initiatives led by Lightmatter, Broadcom's multi-generation roadmap) mature as planned, optical I/O could become deeply embedded at the package level by 2030, permanently easing the copper power wall and letting AI clusters scale to hundreds of thousands of accelerators without interconnect becoming the binding constraint. Sustained multi-billion-dollar strategic investments from Nvidia into Lumentum, Coherent and Ayar Labs suggest the capital and demand visibility needed to fund the laser and indium-phosphide capacity this transition requires.
outlook2030.bear: The bear case is that CPO's serviceability and yield tradeoffs prove too costly at data-center scale, keeping pluggable optics dominant far longer than roadmaps suggest and leaving the industry chronically capacity-constrained on high-power lasers and InP wafers. A slower-than-expected CPO ramp, combined with geopolitical risk around Chinese transceiver suppliers who still hold a large share of global shipments, could leave Western networking supply chains bottlenecked and margins compressed by 2030.

segments.synthesis: Server OEMs and data center operators are riding a second wave of AI capex upgrades: Dell and HPE both raised full-year guidance and saw double-digit stock pops on record AI server backlogs, while Equinix used its first-ever customer summit to push into AI inference and complete a $4B Nordic acquisition. Meanwhile the operator layer is being reshaped by a private-equity-to-public pivot, with Vantage, CyrusOne and Switch all lining up IPOs even as projects like QTS's $30B Virginia campus get killed by permitting and community pushback, showing capital availability is outrunning physical siting capacity.

outlook2030.bull: If prefabricated, modular construction (Compass's industrialized build model, STACK's standardized campuses) and creative power procurement (on-site turbines, direct utility risk-sharing, securitized financing) keep scaling, developers could close the multi-year gap between AI demand and gigawatt-scale delivery, letting the sector's now-abundant private capital (IPOs, ABS, pension co-investment) convert into shipped capacity rather than stalled permits.
outlook2030.bear: The layer's bottleneck is shifting from capital to physical siting: rising state-level moratoria, grid interconnection queues, and community opposition (as seen in QTS's Virginia campus collapse) could strand billions in committed capital, while heavily leveraged financing structures (ABS, construction loans, IPO debt paydown) leave operators exposed if AI demand growth or hyperscaler capex decelerates before campuses reach full utilization.

signals.text: SpaceXAI's Colossus 2 facility in Memphis became operational on September 3, 2026 and is now the world's largest AI data center at roughly 946MW with about $35.8 billion in capital investment.

HPE shares jumped over 7% in premarket trading after its fiscal Q3 2026 earnings combined with renewed attention to its new Nvidia Vera CPU server, and the company raised its fiscal 2026 revenue growth forecast to 34%-37% on record AI server and networking demand, with networking revenue up 75% to $2.9 billion.
Dell Technologies raised its annual revenue outlook by $25 billion, guiding to roughly $192 billion in fiscal 2027 revenue including $74 billion from AI server sales, sending shares to new highs.

Equinix used its inaugural Horizon customer event to launch Equinix Fabric One and an Inference Exchange built with NVIDIA and Together AI, while separately completing a $4 billion acquisition of Nordic operator atNorth alongside CPP Investments.
Supermicro guided to $14.5-15.5 billion in net sales for its fiscal Q1 2027, reporting $7.5 billion in cash against $8.7 billion in bank debt and convertible notes as of June 30, 2026.

segments.label: Servers / DC

rows: OEM AI Servers (Dell PowerEdge, Supermicro, HPE ProLiant)

Shipping Blackwell Ultra/GB300 racks at scale; Dell raised FY27 revenue outlook to ~$192B including $74B of AI servers, HPE lifted FY26 growth guidance to 34-37% on record AI server and networking demand
Vera Rubin NVL72/NVL144 and Vera CPU platforms in volume, rack-scale liquid-cooled systems (Dell PowerRack, HPE AI Grid) become the default enterprise deployment unit
Fully disaggregated, rack-as-a-unit architectures standard; CPU-GPU co-design and optical interconnects mainstream as OEMs compete on total-cost-per-token rather than box specs
Hyperscale Campus Developers (Vantage, QTS, Compass, STACK)
Multi-gigawatt build-outs continue but face growing permitting and community friction, e.g. QTS pulled its $30B Digital Gateway project in Virginia after losing its zoning appeal
IPO/monetization wave matures (Vantage, CyrusOne targeting listings) alongside novel power-procurement structures like on-site gas turbines and utility risk-sharing deals
Consolidation likely among the largest platforms; power availability, not construction speed, is the binding constraint on further campus growth
Colocation & AI Interconnection (Equinix, CoreSite, DataBank, Switch)
Pivot from pure colocation to AI inference and interconnection fabric, e.g. Equinix's new Inference Exchange and Fabric One products launched at its first Horizon event
Metro-edge inference nodes proliferate as enterprises move AI workloads out of hyperscaler clouds; further M&A consolidation (atNorth, Switch IPO) reshapes ownership
Interconnection/inference fabric becomes a distinct utility layer sitting between hyperscale training campuses and enterprise edge deployments
Space & Novel Compute (SpaceX/SpaceXAI)
Now publicly traded (Nasdaq: SPCX); Colossus 2 in Memphis became the world's largest AI data center at ~946MW and $35.8B capex, monetized via GPU-rental deals with Google, Anthropic and Reflection AI
FCC-filed orbital data center constellation begins early pilot compute payloads riding Starlink V3 launches, contingent on Starship reusability

Orbital AI compute clusters potentially operational at meaningful (multi-hundred-MW) scale if cost-per-kW parity with terrestrial sites is achieved, though this remains the most speculative segment of the layer

segments.synthesis: Hyperscaler cloud growth reaccelerated sharply in Q2 CY2026, with Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure both posting their fastest growth in years while combined Big Tech AI capex guidance pushed toward $700-800B for 2026, yet free cash flow at Amazon and Alphabet is compressing hard as spending outruns revenue recognition. Neoclouds CoreWeave and Nebius rode the same wave with triple-digit revenue growth and swelling backlogs, but their debt-heavy financing models drew fresh scrutiny in mid-August when rising rates triggered a sharp, if brief, selloff. The layer's central tension is now financing structure rather than demand: backlogs are enormous and real, but converting them into cash without over-leveraging balance sheets is the swing factor for 2027-2028.

outlook2030.bull: By 2030, hyperscaler and Oracle backlogs measured in the hundreds of billions convert into recognized, high-margin recurring revenue as data center energization and GPU supply catch up to demand, and neocloud financing structures (prepaid contracts, investment-grade asset-backed debt) prove durable enough to fund gigawatt-scale buildouts without credit events.
outlook2030.bear: The bear case is a financing and utilization mismatch: if inference/training demand growth decelerates or GPU generations depreciate faster than debt amortizes, heavily levered neoclouds and Oracle's aggressive OCI buildout could face refinancing stress, forcing write-downs or consolidation, while hyperscalers see capex outpace monetizable revenue and margins compress industry-wide.

signals.text: CoreWeave's Q2 2026 revenue more than doubled to $2.58 billion, beating estimates, and the company disclosed new business wins with Anthropic and Meta during the quarter, pushing its backlog to $104 billion.

Nebius shares plunged 14% in a single session in mid-August after the company issued a $4.5 billion convertible bond, with total liabilities having climbed from $5.29 billion to $17.62 billion in three quarters amid broader market doubts about neocloud financing.

Oracle overshot its own guidance by spending $55.7 billion on data center capital expenditure in fiscal 2026 and now plans to raise roughly $40 billion more in debt and equity, sending shares down 7% on the disclosure.

Microsoft's Q4 FY26 results showed Azure revenue growth accelerating to 43%, commercial remaining performance obligations reaching $678 billion, and capex including finance leases hitting $41 billion for the quarter, up 69% year-over-year.

Google Cloud's growth jumped to 82% in the second quarter of 2026, its fastest pace since at least 2020, after growing 63% the prior quarter, as Alphabet raised full-year capex guidance toward $180-190 billion.

segments.label: Cloud

rows: Hyperscaler Cloud Platforms (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud)
Reaccelerating growth (Azure +43%, Google Cloud +82%, AWS +37%) with combined 2026 capex near $580-700B and RPO backlogs of $460-678B
Backlogs begin converting to recognized revenue at scale; capex growth likely persists but with more scrutiny on time-to-energize and return per dollar
Capacity broadly catches up to demand in mature markets; custom silicon (TPU, Trainium) reduces per-unit AI serving costs and reshapes hyperscaler margin structure
Enterprise/Database-anchored Cloud (Oracle)
OCI scaling fast off a small base, GPU revenue +177%, FY26 capex $55.7B against a $638B RPO, funded via heavy debt and equity issuance
Financing tested as Oracle targets ~$70B net capex outlay in FY2027 with continued debt/equity raises; execution risk on power and construction pace
OCI either cements itself as a genuine fourth hyperscaler with profitable AI workloads or remains capital-constrained relative to peers
Public AI-Native Neoclouds (CoreWeave, Nebius, IREN)
Triple-digit revenue growth, ballooning backlogs ($104B at CoreWeave), but heavy leverage and volatile stock reactions to financing questions
Differentiation via power procurement speed and prepayment-backed contracts (Nebius model) vs. pure debt-funded buildout (CoreWeave)
Consolidation likely; survivors convert multi-year backlogs into durable, profitable capacity as GPU generations and financing structures mature
Private Neoclouds & Emerging Entrants (Lambda, Crusoe, Groq, Nscale)
Massive private rounds and asset-backed debt (Lambda's $926M term loan B, Crusoe's 4.9GW contracted pipeline) ahead of expected IPOs
Several expected to go public (Lambda, Nscale) testing whether private neocloud economics hold up under public market scrutiny
Either integrated into the broader public neocloud/hyperscaler ecosystem via IPO/M&A or squeezed out by oversupply and pricing pressure

segments.synthesis: The application layer is compounding on two axes at once: frontier labs are shipping new flagship models almost monthly (GPT-6 Astra, Claude Fable/Mythos 5.1, Gemini 3.7/3.8 Flash, Grok 4.6) while enterprise incumbents (Salesforce, ServiceNow, Adobe, Microsoft) are converting agentic AI into real, fast-growing recurring revenue lines rather than pilots. At the same time, two IPO trains — OpenAI toward a reported $1T target and Anthropic toward a rumored $2T target as soon as October — are forcing public markets to price frontier-lab economics for the first time, even as reports of enterprises defecting to 'good enough' open-weight models introduce a genuine margin-compression risk.

outlook2030.bull: If agentic products keep converting into durable recurring revenue at the pace Salesforce, Glean, and Harvey are showing today, application-layer AI clears its biggest bottleneck — monetization — well before 2030, and IPOs from OpenAI and Anthropic validate trillion-dollar valuations with real audited financials rather than projections. Vertical AI (legal, creative, IT/security) could reach the kind of embedded, seat-replacing status enterprise software achieved with SaaS, but on a compressed timeline.
outlook2030.bear: The bear case is margin compression from 'good enough' open-weight models undercutting frontier labs on price just as they need to prove profitability to public investors, compounded by OpenAI's own disclosed ~$1.22 loss per dollar of revenue and multi-year path to profitability. A wave of IPOs at stretched multiples, paired with any slowdown in enterprise agent ROI or a safety/regulatory shock, could trigger a sharp re-rating across the whole application layer rather than an orderly maturation.

signals.text: Salesforce raised its fiscal 2027 revenue guidance to $46.1–$46.4 billion after Agentforce ARR surpassed $1.5 billion, up more than 240% year-over-year, alongside 11% quarterly revenue growth.
Adobe's AI-first annualized recurring revenue tripled year-over-year to past $500 million even as its stock trades near multi-year lows and 21% below its 52-week high.

Google DeepMind is preparing to release a coding-focused Gemini 3.8 Flash model, internally tested to be preferred over Anthropic's Claude Opus on coding tasks, following Gemini 3.7 Flash's general availability on August 13.

ServiceNow expanded its Autonomous Workforce with new AI specialists for IT, CRM, employee service, and security/risk, with the security and risk specialists reaching general availability in September 2026.
Microsoft added Python-powered data analysis to Copilot in Excel and made Anthropic's Claude Sonnet 5 a selectable higher-reasoning model inside Word, per its August-to-September release notes.

Enterprise software re-architected around autonomous agents as the default interface rather than dashboards and forms

Fast vertical adoption: Harvey live at 50%+ of Am Law 100 and inside GE Aerospace; Adobe's AI-first ARR tripled past $500M
Vertical AI expands into more regulated domains (healthcare, financial services) with domain-tuned, audited models

Hybrid on-device/cloud compute, agentic 'computer use' and shopping/finance integrations, new image/video model iterations (Midjourney V8.2)
